text:
Let’s discuss how Georgia could approach funding key policy priorities like fully expanding Medicaid.

There is a demonstrated solution with strong bipartisan support. And this is the year to move on it.

Georgia needs to modernize its state cigarette tax.

https://t.co/8MKXeDGU6E

Georgia has the second lowest cigarette tax in the nation. The national average excise tax for a pack of cigarettes is $2.06.

Georgia’s cigarette tax, last updated in 2003, is 37 cents.

Obviously, most states and DC not only have much higher cigarette excise taxes, but have updated them multiple time since Georgia last did.

They reason they have done so is that the policy benefits are apparent.

First, note that smoking harms nearly every organ in the body, and is the leading cause of preventable disease and death worldwide. This creates an incredibly costly health burden on society, and is linked to not just lung and heart disease, but stroke, vascular disease, Type II diabetes, pregnancy risks, and at least a dozen forms of cancer.

https://t.co/IbtauH3TQ5

Adjusting the state tax for cigarettes, even if just to more proportionately mirror the federal excise tax or the cost of a pack of cigarettes, DECREASES SMOKING RATES.

People are less likely to choose to smoke when a pack of cigarettes costs more.

This disincentivizing effect is particularly pronounced for younger smokers, who are more sensitive to price. Consider the decades of health, quality of life, and decreased health costs incurred when you can discourage a young person from smoking.

https://t.co/arl0oDulQx

Second, decreasing smoking rates LOWERS THE STATE HEALTH COSTS RELATED TO SMOKING. The fewer people who choose to smoke, the lower the cost of taking care of preventable smoking related conditions.

Fewer cancer surgeries. Fewer cardiac interventions. Fewer amputations. Fewer long NICU stays for preterm births or ER visits for childhood asthma.

RAISING THE STATE CIGARETTE TAX WOULD SAVE THE STATE MONEY.

https://t.co/IrGTwP0Cy9

It’s important to note here that Medicaid patients smoke at rates twice as high as that of the commercial payor population. That means that at present, THE STATE IS SUBSIDIZING THE PREVENTABLE HEALTH COSTS OF PEOPLE WHO CHOOSE TO SMOKE.

And certainly, people can make the choice to smoke if they want. But it’s reasonable for the state to levy a “users fee” for making a very costly health choice rather than to stick all Georgia taxpayers with those avoidable medical bills.

Third—and here’s where this post began—MODERNIZING GEORGIA’S CIGARETTE TAX GENERATES REVENUE.

How much revenue, you ask? Enough to cover the cost of full Medicaid expansion?

YES.

In this fiscal note from the Georgia DOR, requested by my friend Senator Chuck Hufstetler, Republican Chair of the Georgia Senate Finance Committee, raising the state cigarette excise tax to $1.92 per pack (slightly lower than the national average) would generate $425 million in the first year alone.

https://t.co/45Ge444EiK

Modernizing the state tax for vaping products? Would generate another $97 million that first year.

So raising the state excise tax on tobacco products? It’s a win-win-win.

1.) Lower Georgia’s smoking rates.

2.) Lower state medical costs.

3.) Raise revenue to fund full Medicaid expansion.

Making a plan to reinvest cigarette excise tax revenue back into our public health system and improving access to health coverage for Georgians doesn’t just make logical sense.

It’s our responsibility, and a moral imperative.

That’s how we can move forward in building a healthier Georgia.

And that’s how we can pay for it.

text:
#Allergic #rhinitis and #chronic #rhinosinusitis are common, frequently coexisting upper airway inflammatory diseases linked by shared type 2 immune mechanisms. However, broad variations in sensitisation patterns and treatment response obscure optimal surgical and pharmacological dosing. Advancing care relies on integrating prospective real-world data, non-invasive biomarkers, and personalized treatment.

In this issue, Lundberg and van Waterschoot et al. review surgical options for refractory non-allergic rhinitis in an EAACI Task Force position paper, from inferior turbinate reduction to posterior nasal nerve ablation. Sousa-Pinto et al. use a dose-response network meta-analysis to show that doubling the dose of intranasal medications outperforms adding oral antihistamines in allergic rhinitis, whereas adding intranasal corticosteroids to oral antihistamines outperforms doubling the antihistamine dose. Sola-Martínez and Zubiaga-Fernandez et al. report that exhaled decane and nonadecane may serve as non-invasive biomarkers distinguishing allergic from non-allergic individuals among patients with chronic rhinitis. Cardoso et al. show in a randomised, placebo-controlled trial that eight week supplementation with a heat-treated Bifidobacterium longum CECT 7347 postbiotic significantly reduced combined symptom and medication scores in adults with allergic rhinitis. Campion et al. show that out-of-season high-dose nasal birch pollen challenge raises allergen-specific IgE and effector cell sensitivity, while later attenuating the seasonal amplification of allergic responses in birch pollen-allergic adults. Leily et al. demonstrate that in the Isle of Wight birth cohort persistent Alternaria sensitisation from childhood to adulthood correlates with persistent asthma and, more strongly, rhinitis. Virkkula et al. report in a randomised controlled trial that full and limited endoscopic sinus surgery both improve quality of life in chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps, without a significant difference between the two approaches at 24 months. Bärhold et al. show that simultaneous dual type 2 biologic therapy improves sinonasal outcomes in selected patients with severe uncontrolled chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps and type 2 comorbidities. Dramburg and Hernandez Toro et al. use prospective e-Diary data from the @IT.2020 project to classify seasonal allergic rhinitis into mild, moderate, and severe clusters, revealing substantial recall bias in the retrospective ARIA classification. Sousa-Pinto et al. use MASK-air app data to show that both as-needed and regular medication use in the pollen season can achieve good symptom control and treatment satisfaction in allergic rhinitis. Hasegawa et al. link complement activation to fibrin deposition through complement-eosinophil crosstalk in eosinophilic chronic rhinosinusitis. Bousquet et al. discuss the need to assess on-demand versus continuous treatment in allergic rhinitis in the ARIA-EAACI guidelines. Han et al. report that increased cell adhesion molecule 5 expression in nasal polyps is associated with plasma cell infiltration.
